full_text: Nice idea, but poorly designed PCI and SATA layout I was very excited about my purchase of the MSI 970 Gaming Motherboard, as I have been using their MSI 770-C45 MoBo for several years and have really enjoyed it's performance and reliability. Time goes on, and I wanted USB 3.0. Unfortunately, due to the layout of the 770-C45 Motherboard, with only one PCIe x16 slot and two X1 slots, I hit a brick wall. The graphics controller (GEFORCE GT 640) works fine in the one PCIe x16 slot, but it covers one of the only two X1 slots because of it's size. The other available x1 slot is in use with a Promise FastTrak TX4650 RAID Controller (unfortunately, now EOSL) and after buying an x1 USB 3.0 card I opened case and realized that I did not have an available PCIe slot to install USB 3.0 card in. So I purchased the 970 Gaming Motherboard along with 4x4GB RAM DIMMS (were 2GB), very excited about prospect of using existing AMD Phenom II 3ghz processor (for AM3 or AM3+, can't recall but MoBo says it supports both sockets) in new 970 Gaming system, along with the GEFORCE 640 video controller, giving me USB 3.0, two large PCIe slots (one X16, other X8). Unfortunately, the way the designers layed out the PCI slots, the graphics module in the X16 slot is double-wide and covers one of the PCIe X1 slots (they should have covered one of the 3 obsolete PCI slots) so that left me with a PCIe X8 and a PCIe X1 (which I moved the Promise RAID controller on to. I have a rather roomy PC case, an ULTRA X-Blaster ATX Mid-Tower and did not anticipate problems. The horizontal drive bays in the front of the case holds (top to bottom) a SATA SDD (100 GB system drive), a DVD player/recorder, a Blu-Ray player/recorder, and two additional 3.5 drives used for surveillance and backups. At the bottom of the Ultra Mid-Tower is a compartment for four more 3.5 drives, currently populated with 3x2TB drives connected to the Promise RAID controller in a RAID-1 (Mirror) configuration, with one drive as a hot-standby if one drive fails. This RAID array contains everything but the system programs which are on the SDD... The Documents, Music, Pictures and Videos paths all go down to the 2TB mirror-set) This is where my grief comes in (besides one PCIe X1 slot covered by the double-wide graphics card in the X16 slot): The previous MSI 770-C45 had the SATA ports (for the system disk, DVD and BD drives and the other two) all facing UP from the motherboard, 90 degrees vertical in relationship to the surface of the motherboard. The much-anticipated 970 Gaming MoBo has the six SATA 6GB ports in a horizontal configuration, facing front, from the opposite side of the I/O and PCI external connectors at the back... These horizontal connectors are at the "front" of the motherboard, with only about 3/4" clearance before the internal cabinet rack that holds the RAID drives. MSI was kind enough to include two SATA cables, one was straight to straight, the other 90-degrees to straight (.5 meters). Unfortunately, the elbow connector points in a "down" orientation (into the floor of the cabinet) rather than 'up', and the SATA connectors are 2 high by 3 wide, with no horizontal stagger if I wanted to buy some elbow cables in the "up" orientation (one would fit, above, but not the one below, so will only be able to connect 3 drives in current mounting). So, what was thought to be a rather roomy configuration for this motherboard was anything but. I have an excellent Rosewill XTreame power supply (RX850-S-B which has a combined power of 850 Watts), with the primary ATX 24 pin power connector as well as a secondary 8 pin connector providing four more 12v power sources. I did not have to use the 8 pin power connector from the Rosewill PS with the previous MSI motherboard, but it was there, along with two 6 pin power connectors. So I connected the 8 pin supply cable in the JPWR2 socket as instructed in the guide. Without 90-degree SATA cables pointing "up" from the MoBo, I tried to connect straight ones, having to bend them quite severely (even past the recommended 90 degree limit) in order to plug in two cables for the system disk and the DVD, to try to get it up and running while looking for extender elbows or other alternatives. Well, a long story short, I've got a system that powers up for one second and then off. I turn off the PS via the rear power switch, unplug the PS, plug it back in and turn it on. I push the front panel power button and on every occasion, it comes up long enough to spin the fans and then shuts itself back down. No video output, so no clue what the problem is, except perhaps a faulty 8 pin Rosewill power cable or damaged SATA cables in my over-bending attempt to get something working. I don't know what the designers were thinking when they pointed the SATA connecters "out" rather than "up". An extreme disappointment. I should have noticed the changed orientation of the SATA connectors and looked at the board size in the specifications, opened up my case, and ensured that there would be clearance, but I was an optimist and, since the SATA connectors on the other board were vertical it didn't even cross my mind, until I installed the board. Very disappointing day... Tomorrow (today now) I will triple-check all connections, verify voltage on the not-used-before 8-pin JPWR2 connector to ensure it's providing 12v and purchase 3 up-facing SATA cables to see if I can salvage something of this debacle. I'll also be looking for extended elbows so the bottom SATA connectors can be used. I am also seriously considering returning the 970 Gaming and asking for a refund. If running, it may scream like a wild ape, and be ready for a future processor and video controller upgrades, but now, the PC I've been nurturing for almost 20 years, incrementally improving HW and upgrading Operating Systems over time, is now a boat anchor. Two terrible design decisions, forcing me to cover a PCIe X1 slot with the video card, and the inferior orientation of the SATA connectors cause me to give this two stars.

full_text: Get this if you sing in a local band! To sing in tune you really need to hear yourself over the band. I have tried all kinds of solutions for on stage monitoring. Wedges, wireless in ear, etc. Wedges on stage have a lot of problems. They never seem loud enough, but if you get them loud they squeal with feedback. Especially if there are more than one singers and wedges. And a huge problem with wedges is that they cause a volume competition, raising the stage volume. Not to mention they are large and heavy. Personal in ear monitors are the choice of the stars, who can afford to have a sound engineer who is dedicated to delivering a perfect mix of singer and band to the in ear monitors. But when you play in a local band, the sound company often times does not have the skill to make a nice personal mix for in ear monitors. Or you might be playing through your own small PA that does not have much of a monitor section. In ears give the best monitoring, but to use them it seems like you have to have a sophisticated monitor mix, which is not really available to local musicians. In order to solve this I have been using the best quality single ear headphone I could find, and then I would be able to hear the band and also my own voice. My signal chain is from the mic I have a 10' XLR cable into a Rolls PM55 personal monitor. The signal is passed by the PM55 to the PA system in the XLR through. I connect an Elite Core Body pack to the headphone send of the PM55, and so I have my own self contained wired in ear monitor system that requires no help from the sound engineer. I installed the PM55 on my guitar pedal board. The problem has been the actual earphones. The mono system was better than wedges but still was not right. I looked at custom earphones but it looked complicated. The Westones seemed super pricey, but in desperation I ordered them. My official report is that they do the job really well. They allow the stage sounds to come through, so you can hear the rest of the band. I suppose they attenuate the local sound a little bit, but in a rehearsal you hear the other musicians talking just fine. And they have a very good sound. The PM55 gets them to be quite loud. So, yes, now you can have your own personal in ear monitor, independent of the sound engineer, and also hear the band on stage. The way they wrap over your ear takes some getting used to, but I think it is the best system. They are comfortable and the wire hides out of the way, and the plugs don't fall out. They come with a bunch of alternative foam surrounds, but for me the defaults were fine. And they come with a nice box to keep in the gig bag. It seems that the cable can be replaced, but I have not tried. It is nice that Westone is an old line company that will probably be in business when I need to buy replacement parts. They still seem expensive, but they are worth the money if you sing in tune. I don't know of any alternatives that would be as good. The one downside is that they don't block much sound, so the guitar player still can seem way too loud. But that is part of the deal I suppose, since the whole point is to pass the ambient sound. Oh yeah, the other complaint is that the cable seems to twist itself into knots when you put the earplugs in the little orange box. Sometimes I have to take several minutes unwinding the knot in order to use them. So I would buy them again, and I recommend them to anyone who is a singer in a "local" band. Worth the hefty price.

Rather than hauling a 15.6-inch laptop at 5-ish pounds plus a power brick, this T100 is far more sensible. I had faith the Atom processor would ably run Windows 10 based on previous experience with an Intel NUC, and I found that Windows 10 runs all my apps on the T100 with reasonable speed and responsiveness. Video calls on Skype work well. I bought the T100 for about $USD160 on sale at the Amazon Warehouse. When I bought the T100, I wanted a lightweight laptop to serve as a "beater" for travelling. My requirements were: cheap, lightweight (about 2 pounds), Windows 10 (I love Android, but I rely on Office and other Windows apps, so a Chromebook seemed like an unnecessary limitation), 64 GB on-board storage (a clean Windows 10 + Office 2010 can be as much as 20-23 GB), minimum 10.1-inch screen, micro-USB charging (no more power brick!), wireless, and a keyboard. The T100 filled these specs, but it should be understood that the T100 is really a tablet with a proprietary detachable keyboard (rather than a fold-over, like a Lenovo Yoga). Wireless has been solid, battery life has been excellent (easily replenished with USB power banks and chargers), and the Windows 10 touchscreen interface is pretty decent (even for taking notes). Bluetooth is also available for when you want to rock a mouse. I had heard good things about the keyboard, and I found it to be very good, although I usually don't preoccupy myself with the keyboard experience. The accessibility tools in Windows 10 are handy when I need to magnify the screen for close work. Should you run out of room on the installed drive, the T100 has an SD card slot for extra room. Happily, the repaired T100 ran perfectly and has been completely reliable. My hat's off to Asus support for the double-RMA. One more point: the T100 runs 32-bit Windows 10. I have considered upgrading to 64-bit, which should be possible, but on an Atom processor the prospects for improved performance seemed dim, plus I was concerned that there would be no 64-bit driver support. 32-bit has been working fine.

full_text: Issues with older spinning drives This is for the model EC-U30 with this description "[Upgraded Version Support UASP] Sabrent Ultra Slim USB 3.0 to 2.5-Inch SATA External Aluminum Hard Drive Enclosure [Silver Aluminum Finish] (EC-UM30)" from vendor Sabrent. I am having multiple issues and will be ordering a replacement from another company today. Here are the issues: 1. The interior width of the enclosure is too tight. Drives scrape going in, and taking them out takes some prying. This is with a Seagate 2.5" standard drive and less so but still an issue with a new Transcend SSD. 2. The drive connects intermittently with the Seagate standard drive, and I think I know why: The enclosure came with a cable that had a single A-Type USB Male on both ends, and for a standard spinning drive, it really needs the dual plugs on one end to supply the power needed for the drive to spin up. See, a cable with two plugs on one end gets power from two USB ports. One end is usually red, which is just power, the other is normal, power and data. Unfortunately, the cables I have with the dual plug have a mini-USB on the enclosure end, so they won't work for me. By the way, an SSD drive doesn't need that burst of power to spin up, so the cable would work fine for SSD's. Bottom line: If you are using this for an SSD, and don't plan on disassembling it frequently, you will be fine. Otherwise, I recommend a different product.

full_text: Completely unreliable I have two of these cameras purchased 45 days apart and there are several problems that come out after some time. First, you are supposed to be notified by email whenever a motion is detected in the cameras field of view, but it happens not only when there is actual movement, but also by any change in the lighting intensity over the area covered by the camera. It happens at sunset, sunrise and whenever an exterior light is turned on or off. Decreasing the sensitivity down to as low as 5 % doesn't solve the problem. Second, the email notification for motion detection may take from 10 to 120 seconds since an actual event triggers the alarm. This may be related to the D-Link servers but in 2 minutes you may miss something important going on. Third, the cameras signal gets disconnected and an email notification is sent, but during that moment you can't access the video feed from the camera and it last several minutes. Some times it reconnects by themselves but others you have to unplug them from the power line, wait 1 minute, and plug them back, but as it happened last week, both cameras were disconnected over 8 times in a 2 hours period while I was homr,and would not reconnect even trying the power off-on troubleshooting. During that time I checked both the router and the modem and all the wi-fi gadgets that were connected to the router had a strong signal.. For this latest problem D-Link tech support suggested re-flashing the firmware of the cameras, which implies taking them down from where they are installed. connect them to a computer with an ethernet cable and repeat a process that, for both cameras, each took me a terrible ordeal and 2 good hours of patience and phone connection to the tech support number in a very frustrating process. Adding all this three problems it is evident that you can't rely on them as a surveillance system: the false alarms may get you to the moral of the 'cry wolf' children tale; the delay in some email notifications don't help make me fell confident and the cameras getting disconnected at random when you are not home really make me regret the purchase of these cameras. So, if you are looking to an alternative to a paid alarm monitoring system, you better look somewhere else.

full_text: Doesn't Help Ultraslim Drives Fit Most Laptops This product, combined with the ultraslim hard drive it's meant to work with, is very disappointing. I purchased a WD Ultraslim hard drive without realizing just what it was. It didn't seem right to try to return it, since if I had read the listing more carefully, I would have learned from the seller that Ultraslim drives are proprietary fit for laptops that originally came with such drives, so instead I decided to buy an adapter so I could use it in a standard SATA bay. So far, though, no dice. Although the adapter does, indeed, allow the drive to fit a standard SATA socket, this one seems to be oriented the wrong way for most laptop drive bays. I've tried them in several laptops from different manufacturers, and in each one, the drive + adapter didn't line up properly with the screw holes in the sled, and thus wouldn't fit properly in the drive bay. Almost as bad, there is nothing at all other than the Ultraslim data/power connector holding the drive and adapter together. That doesn't bode well for mobile use. I will probably have to use something like mounting tape to make sure the drive doesn't unplug from the adapter when the computer is moved. And given the fact that it doesn't seem to actually fit in any laptop drive bays, I suspect I'll end up using it with a 2.5" to 3.5" bay adapter and putting it into a desktop. 12/10/2016: SNANSHI reached out to me with a refund offer. I declined, because in order to make use of my Ultraslim drive, I will need some sort of adapter, and all the adapters I've seen that appear to be designed to allow an Ultraslim drive to be used with a conventional laptop appear to be basically the same as this one. But since I think it's important to acknowledge and appreciate it when a company stands behind its products, I have increased my rating from 2 stars to 3. The adapter DOES work. It's just not well suited to my particular need.

full_text: Windows saved Samsung's Installation Problem I build my own PCs and tend to overbuild them so they will last. The one I use for myself I built about 4-5 years when SSD drives were more expensive. So I bought a relatively small SSD drive (512 GB) for my primary drive (so it would boot fast and load my programs quickly), but put in two other regular hard drives as well (one for my data and one for an internal backup). Last week I started having significant problems and realized I was almost out of disc space on my SSD drive. Prices are much cheaper now, so I bought a Samsung 1 Terabyte SSD drive. I didn't want to waste a day reinstalling all my programs, so I cloned the old SSD drive to the new one using the software that came with the drive. Then I swapped drives and turned the PC on. No go - there was no bootable drive installed. I was not thinking kind things about the Samsung program, so I booted up with the original Windows 7 disc. It's repair feature found a minor problem, fixed it, and then everything worked fine. All of my program files are now on the new drive and it works great. So I'm happy with the drive and mostly satisfied with Samsung's cloning program. Not sure why or how it generated an error, but glad Microsoft's free repair program was enough to fix it. I also bought this cable (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00XLAZODE/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o02_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) to make the cloning as easy as possible. I didn't even need to open up my PC until I swapped drives.

full_text: Quirky, multiple problems If you manage to get a reliable board, you will be happy, but good luck with that. I initially had issues with the BMC management on this board. The RAM voltages are hard-coded, so if you have low voltage RAM installed, the BMC alarms would alert because low-voltage RAM by default runs at lower voltage normally. So I couldn't use the BMC monitoring or I would have all these false alerts. Contacted ASRock support, no solution to customize the voltage alert level. Then, Intel has announced that some faulty silicon was used on the C2000 CPUs which can result in premature failure. I RMAd the board, and received the answer due to the BMC alarm issue they would replace it, but not necessarily for the Intel-announced problem. So I receive the new board (I have to pay for the shipping to RMA the board, ASRock covers return shipping), and ASRock support said that the board that has the replaced silicon is version 1.03 of the board, which is what I received. I RMA'd version1.02 of the board. I install the board with all the same RAM, hard drives, etc. and the board won't finish the POST process, it is stuck on "system initializing." Can't get to the BMC, can't get to the BIOS. Googling this, apparently this is a common issue. Some people say they have to RMA their board. I found a forum posting that said to pull the CMOS battery for 15 minutes and remove all the RAM but 1 stick. Put the CMOS battery back in and then boot. This time it did finally boot after going through one or two self-reboots. I powered off and added the 2nd stick of RAM that was previously working in this system with no problems. Back to being stuck on system initializing. I was thinking the 2nd stick of RAM is bad (that would be odd but not impossible even though it was working with the old board), so I pulled the first stick and only used the second stick, and the system booted. So RAM isn't bad. Added the other stick of RAM and this time the system booted. I would think I didn't have the RAM seated properly, but its not like I am new at this, have built a fair number of servers and desktops. This board is finicky, and it wasn't cheap. I have zero confidence in this board. This is the first time I have purchased an ASRock board, I usually get Gigabyte or Intel. I don't think I will be trying ASRock again after using this board.

The only issue I have with the Cinegrey screen material is that it has a sparkly sheen to it. I have a short throw projector so I knew to stay away from the Cinegrey 3D but the material that I received has the sparkly effect that you would expect to see from a 3D or high gain material. It's more prominent when sitting directly in front of the screen and seems to show in the center.. I'm not sure if this was a mixup from the manufacturer or if this is the way that Cinegrey looks.
